scenes.narration: Nobody writes everything from scratch. Today we learn to borrow code, from Python and from our own files.

scenes.onScreen: "Borrowing code": three numbered lines (1. import module makes its names available as module.name; 2. from module import name brings one name in directly; 3. Every .py file is a module) and an analogy card: a toolbox in a garage: you fetch the box you need, and use the tools inside
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A module is a file of ready-made code. Import brings it in. After import math, you write math, a dot, and the name you want. From math import floor brings floor in directly, with no prefix. Python ships with hundreds of modules, called the standard library. Think of a toolbox in a garage. You fetch the box you need, and use the tools inside. Any dot py file you write is also a module, if it sits in the same folder.

lines: import module makes its names available as module.name
from module import name brings one name in directly

[HL 7] And pi, with every digit a float can hold.

code.source:
import shacktools
print(shacktools.label("Baga"))
import math
print(math.sqrt(16))
from shacktools import label
print(label("Colva"))
print(math.pi)

scenes.onScreen: A search path: the current folder first, then the standard library, then installed packages
scenes.animation: A path of three boxes lights up in order; a matching box stops the search
scenes.narration: Here is where Python looks. First, the folder of your script. Then the standard library. Then the packages you installed. The first match wins. So never name your own file the same as a standard module, like random or math. Your file hides the real one. Then strange errors follow.

lines: First, the folder of your script.

scenes.onScreen: alias.py: import with as, and from with several names
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] Import math, and give it the short name m. [HL 2] From math, import floor and ceil, two names at once. [HL 3] Use the alias. Floor of two point seven is two. [HL 4] Use the names directly. Floor gives two, ceil of two point one gives three. Aliases save typing, and from imports save more. Use whichever keeps your code clear.

code.source:
import math as m
from math import floor, ceil
print(m.floor(2.7))
print(floor(2.7), ceil(2.1))

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as alias dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, alias dot py. Two, then two three.

scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: import module gives you module dot name. Two: from module import name gives you name directly. Three: as gives a module a shorter name. Four: Your own dot py file is a module too. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

lines: From module import name gives you name directly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: a module that does not exist
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We import maths, with an s. There is no such module. Python says, module not found error, no module named maths. Check the spelling of the module name. The error shows exactly what it looked for. Fix the name, and the import works.

props.error:
File "usemod.py", line 1, in <module>
    import maths
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'maths'
props.why: Python can only import a module it can find; a misspelled name is not found, so Python raises ModuleNotFoundError.

shorts.title: What is a module?
shorts.hook: "A module is a file of ready-made code."
shorts.script: A module is a file of ready-made code. Import brings it in. After import math, you write math dot sqrt, and Python finds the square root tool inside. Python ships with hundreds of modules, called the standard library. Think of a toolbox in a garage. You fetch the box you need, and use the tools inside, without building them yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Borrow ready-made code.

shorts.title: From import
shorts.hook: "Sometimes you want just one tool from a module."
shorts.script: Sometimes you want just one tool from a module. From math import floor. Now you can write floor directly, with no math prefix. You can import several names at once, separated by commas. It makes code shorter, but the prefix form tells readers where a name came from. Use from imports for a few well-known names, and the prefix form otherwise. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Bring one name in.

shorts.title: Your own modules
shorts.hook: "Every dot py file you write is a module."
shorts.script: Every dot py file you write is a module. Put a function in shacktools dot py. In another file, in the same folder, write import shacktools. Then call shacktools dot label. That is how big programs are split into small files. Never name your file the same as a standard module, like random or math. If you do, you hide the real one. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Your files are modules.

shorts.title: Module not found
shorts.script: The import bug. You write import maths, with an s. Python says, module not found error, no module named maths. The error shows exactly the name it looked for. Check the spelling. Check that the file is in the same folder, if it is your own. And if it is a package, check that you installed it, which we cover in a few episodes. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Check the name.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.script: Why did the programmer love imports? Someone else had already done the hard work. Your challenge. Import the math module. Print the area of a circle with radius three. The formula is pi times radius squared. Round the answer to two decimals. You should see twenty eight point two seven. Share your line of code in the comments below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 56.
shorts.caption: Try math.
